mainText:
If you only remember one thing: A I labs are publishing science at industrial scale, while insiders warn the safety culture can't keep up.

Number one. Open A I's math flood. Open A I published seven hundred nineteen math manuscripts from an unreleased frontier model, with formal proofs for many. The same model produced the Navier Stokes result announced a month ago. An advisory group asked labs not to test on proprietary models the community can't access. Critics say that wasn't followed. Why it matters: science is being produced faster than anyone can verify it.

Number two. Another safety resignation. Open A I safety researcher David Robinson quit. In The Atlantic he wrote that the company's culture is broken. He says labs should run like nuclear plants or airports, with heavy redundancy, and that outside safety incentives are needed. It follows a September resignation at Anthropic. Why it matters: the debate is moving from laws to company culture.

Number three. Open models versus China. Mistral released Large four, nicknamed Le Chonk, a one trillion parameter open model. Reflection A I unveiled Beam, which uses three to four times less compute. Both are pitched as Western alternatives to Chinese open models. Why it matters: open model leadership is now a geopolitical contest.

Number four. Watermarks and the European Union. Google opened its Synth I D detector to the public, with about one million checks a day. Open A I will add invisible watermarks to ChatGPT text in the E U, to meet A I Act rules. Why it matters: regulation is making provenance labels the default.

Number five. Claude Haiku five point five. Anthropic cut prices up to ninety percent for prompts under one hundred thousand tokens. That's ten cents per million input tokens. Open A I's G P T six Luna matches those short prompt rates. Why it matters: cheap small models make always on A I agents affordable.

Number six. Good news. Biohub expanded its virtual biology effort to one point eight billion dollars, with the N I H, the Energy Department, DeepMind, Meta and Isomorphic Labs. The goal is a virtual cell that predicts how cells respond to drugs before lab tests. Why it matters: a moonshot to cure disease is easy to root for.

Also in your Reads. The Rundown on slop grenades, polished A I documents that push work onto the reader. The New Yorker on New York's carriage horses and Anne Carson's Nobel win. And Reframing Climate Change, with an event at Yale on October fifteenth.

The thread today: fast science, thin guardrails, and a race over open models. That's your briefing.
